[C7] After validators run after Pydantic's internal validation, are generally more type-safe and easier to implement, and are suitable for post-parse checks or mutations (and must return the validated value). answer: positive_spans is a list of offset:length pairs that map bucket indices and positive_buckets is a list of observation counts, one entry per bucket [C1]. For float histograms the bucket list elements are the bucket populations directly, while for integer histograms the elements are int64 deltas with the first element an absolute population [C3]. Example: positive_spans:[0:3,2:2] with positive_buckets:[10,15,12,8,12] means indices 0,1,2 populated, then 2 empty buckets, then two more populated buckets, totaling five bucket values matching the five entries [C1].

answer: Native histograms are a structured sample type where a single sample represents sum, count and a dynamic set of buckets and are treated as first-class citizens in Prometheus' data model [C4][C2]. Classic histograms are exposed as multiple float time series: cumulative per-bucket counters <basename>_bucket{le="..."}, plus <basename>_sum and <basename>_count [C2]. Native histograms use a sparse representation, require no predefined bucket boundaries, pick dynamic resolution, offer higher resolution, efficient storage and atomic network transfer, and ensure mergeability between histograms using standard schemas [C4][C2]. Classic histograms require careful predefined bucket layouts, are essentially bucketed counters where labels are multiplicative (cardinality matters), and histograms with different bucket boundaries are not generally aggregatable [C1][C2]. Prometheus can ingest classic histograms as NHCBs (Native Histograms with Custom Bucket boundaries) to get native-like storage and atomicity while keeping the classic bucket layout and its quantile error characteristics [C2][C3]. Prefer native histograms for new instrumentation when your instrumentation library or OpenTelemetry supports them; if you need precise, arbitrary bucket boundaries or cannot migrate immediately, stick with classic histograms or use NHCB conversion while noting migration caveats such as query differences and aggregation difficulties between types [C1][C8][C3].

You should implement this customization when you need more extensive or custom validation/serialization behavior or when creating a true custom type that Pydantic cannot schema-generate itself, but you should prefer built-in high-level hooks (e.g., annotated-types, Field, AfterValidator) or use GetPydanticSchema to reduce boilerplate when possible. answer: Logs are often critical for troubleshooting, while metrics are equally valuable and you typically jump back and forth between different signals during an investigation [C1]. Whenever you log an event, consider counting it by broad category because counting is cheap and gives alerting on elevated error rates plus an overview of what is happening [C1]. A metric without labels is inexpensive, so favor simple counters, but avoid high label cardinality because each labelset is an additional time series with RAM/CPU/disk/network costs and very large cardinality can overwhelm Prometheus [C1][C4]. Prometheus is a system for metrics, not for ingesting raw logs; use systems like Grafana Loki or OpenSearch to handle logs or to extract metrics from them [C2]. Prometheus is also not suitable when you need 100% accurate, detailed, and complete data (for example per-request billing); use another system for that and Prometheus for monitoring [C3]. Expose raw counters (e.g., failed and total requests) rather than derived ratios or averages so ingestors can compute them with better mathematical properties and resilience to scrape failures [C6].

answer: Standard schemas provide dynamic exponential bucketing, require no predefined boundaries, use a sparse representation, and ensure mergeability between histograms using those schemas [C2][C6]. Standard schemas allow higher bucket resolution across ranges at lower storage and query cost and can be reduced on ingestion to satisfy scrape and storage limits [C2][C4]. NHCBs (schema -53) allow explicit custom bucket boundaries and can represent classic histograms or be chosen when exponential bucketing is a poor match [C1][C6]. Different NHCB custom boundaries are generally not mergeable and NHCBs are only compatible with each other; reconciling differing custom values requires merging buckets and can collapse observations into a single overflow bucket, with queries flagged by an info-level annotation [C1][C5]. NHCBs have the same quantile error as classic histograms and behave like classic histograms on the instrumentation side [C7]. Therefore NHCBs SHOULD be used only for informed, specific use cases, while standard schemas are typically preferable for mergeability and dynamic resolution [C1][C3].

answer: Higher capacity reduces the chance that individual shard queues will fill and block WAL reads, preventing throughput from ceasing, but it increases memory consumption and lengthens times to clear queues during resharding [C1][C6][C4]. Lower capacity limits memory use and shortens queue-drain time during resharding but makes it more likely that a filled shard will block WAL reads and halt throughput [C4][C1][C6]. answer: NHCBs are ingested and stored as composite samples represented by a single series, giving them the same storage efficiency and atomic network transfer properties as native histograms rather than the many per-bucket series of classic histograms [C6][C7]. Query performance and number of series for NHCBs match usual native histograms, but the quantile error of NHCBs remains that of the corresponding classic histogram instrumentation [C1]. Native histograms provide sparse representation, dynamic exponential bucketing, mergeability, and higher achievable resolution at lower resource cost, improving monitoring efficiency and aggregatability [C4][C7]. NHCBs still carry classic-bucket limitations: reconciling different bucket layouts can severely reduce resolution and yields info-level annotations on queries, which can harm the usefulness of aggregated queries [C6][C1]. In short, NHCBs give the storage and query-efficiency advantages of native histograms while inheriting the quantile error and bucket-layout fragility of classic histograms, affecting monitoring accuracy when bucket layouts change [C7][C1].

answer: If either histogram is a gauge, counter-reset rules do not apply, and a gauge followed by a counter is treated as a counter reset because the change is equivalent to deleting the gauge and creating a new counter at zero [C1]. For two counter histograms using a standard schema, first check whether schema or zero-bucket-width changes constitute a compatible resolution reduction: the schema number must have decreased between standard exponential schemas, and any populated regular bucket in the first histogram must be either fully included in the second histogram’s zero bucket or not at all [C1]. If those conditions are not met, treat the change as a counter reset [C1]. If they are met, convert the first histogram to match the second by merging neighboring buckets and merging regular buckets into the zero bucket as needed [C1]. After matching schemas and zero-bucket widths, declare a counter reset if the total count drops or if any bucket population (including the zero bucket) drops or a previously populated bucket disappears; a drop in the sum alone does not constitute a reset [C1][C2]. Counter-reset detection is preferably done at ingestion and persisted in histogram flags, but an UnknownCounterReset hint requires the querier to perform detection again [C3]. Start timestamps can also be used by inserting a synthetic zero sample with its counter-reset information set to CounterReset and matching attributes to the following sample [C8].

When moving toward Prometheus‑style or symptom‑focused rules, follow Prometheus best practices such as pre‑aggregating with recording rules, adding label filters, and setting realistic pending periods to limit load and false positives [C2].

Evaluation frequency, result cardinality, and query complexity affect resource consumption, so your choice of where to manage lifetimes can influence load on Grafana and your data sources [C2].

InfluxDB uses a variant of a log‑structured merge tree with a write‑ahead log and time sharding, which suits event logging, while Prometheus uses an append‑only file per time series storage approach. [C3]
For scope and tooling, InfluxDB is commonly considered together with Kapacitor (for continuous queries and alerting), while Prometheus paired with the Alertmanager provides alert grouping, deduplication, silencing and a more powerful query language. [C7]
InfluxDB is maintained by a single commercial company using an open‑core model with commercial clustering and support, whereas Prometheus is a fully open source and independent project maintained by multiple companies and individuals. [C2]

answer: The CompositeValue fields appear in this order: count, sum, schema, zero_threshold, zero_count, positive_spans, positive_buckets. [C3] The count is the total number of observations and sum is the sum of observed values. [C3] The schema is an integer controlling the exponential bucket width, zero_threshold defines the zero bucket boundary, and zero_count is the number of observations in that zero bucket. [C3] Spans are offset:length pairs; the first span's offset is the starting bucket index (can be negative) and its length is the number of consecutive populated buckets, while subsequent spans' offsets indicate how many empty buckets to skip before the next group. [C3][C5] In the example positive_spans:[0:3,2:2] with positive_buckets:[10,15,12,8,12], the first span covers buckets at indices 0,1,2 with counts 10,15,12, then two empty buckets are skipped, then two more consecutive buckets with counts 8 and 12, totaling five buckets which matches the five values in positive_buckets. [C3] If no buckets are populated, the span and bucket fields can be omitted. [C3]

FastAPI recommends using Annotated for query parameters because it preserves the Python function parameter’s actual default and allows multiple metadata annotations for documentation and reuse outside FastAPI (e.g., with other tools). [C1][C3][C8]
Pydantic allows validators via the annotated pattern (e.g., Annotated[..., AfterValidator(...)]) to make validators reusable and to target parts of a type (like list items). [C2][C4]
Pydantic’s @field_validator decorator is designed to apply one function to multiple fields (or '*' for all fields) and offers options like mode and check_fields for class-level validators. [C2]
Pydantic provides distinct validator kinds—after (runs after internal validation), plain (terminates validation immediately), and wrap (can call a handler to delegate to Pydantic)—so you should choose the validator type based on whether you need post-validation checks, to bypass or wrap internal validation, or to mutate values. [C4][C5]
In short: prefer FastAPI’s Annotated for declaring and documenting query parameters and for reusable type-level validators in endpoints, and prefer Pydantic’s @field_validator (and specific validator types/modes) when you need multi-field application, timing/control over validation, or wrapping behavior. Relying on timestamps has caveats: exemplar timestamps may be slightly skewed or truncated across systems causing apparent duplicates or ordering anomalies, and out-of-order exemplars are only considered when all exemplars would be sorted before the last appended exemplar, so mixed out-of-order cases may go undetected and are treated as acceptable [C8][C1].

Native histograms solve the bucket-layout problem of classic histograms because they require no predefined boundaries, adjust resolution dynamically, and use a sparse representation where empty buckets cost nothing [C1][C2].
They are a first-class composite sample type that represents sum and count plus a dynamic set of buckets, enabling higher resolution and lower storage and query cost with very little to no configuration [C2][C3].
Native histograms provide atomic network transfers and are aggregatable across instances via standard exponential bucketing schemas, whereas classic histograms with differing bucket boundaries are not generally aggregatable [C3][C2].
Their sparse and integer/float-aware data representations also improve exposition and storage efficiency (for example via protobuf varint encoding), making partitioning by labels more affordable [C2][C6].
For these reasons, the documentation advises preferring native histograms for new instrumentation when supported by your library [C1][C3].
